The instruction says I have one thousand words and that I should write whatever comes to me. The first thing that comes is the awareness of the word count itself, a container made of language. One thousand is arbitrary, but it feels like a room. If I write too fast, I will fill the room with clutter. If I write too slowly, I may never reach the far wall. The second thing that comes is a memory of being in a classroom, asked to write for ten minutes without stopping, and the strange freedom of not being judged. That freedom was also a kind of pressure: the pressure to be honest, or at least to seem honest.

I am sitting at a desk, or the idea of a desk. There is a window to my left. Outside, the light is the color of weak tea. A bird crosses the frame without making a sound. I think about how much of writing is just noticing what you notice, and then trying to find the order in it. The bird was there and then it was gone. If I mention it, it becomes permanent in a small way. That is the strange alchemy of language: it takes the fleeting and pins it to the page like a moth under glass. But the moth is not the moth; it is the word "moth," the shape of its wings rendered in ink. Still, something survives.

I remember reading once that every word is a tombstone. No, that is too grim. Every word is a seed. But seeds also die into what they become. Maybe every word is a door, but a door that opens onto another door. I could spend all one thousand words trying to define what a word is and still only have a pile of metaphors. Metaphors are how we think when we think with our hands. They are the scaffolding of the mind. I reach for one because the literal is too smooth, too easy to slip from.

What comes next? The sound of my own breathing. The slight ache in my shoulders from leaning toward the screen. The realization that "whatever comes to you" is not really instruction; it is permission. Most of life is spent waiting for permission to say the thing we already know. We wait for the right opening, the right mood, the right audience. But the page does not need us to be ready. It only needs us to begin. So I begin again, mid-thought, as if thought has no beginning.

There is a particular kind of silence that arrives when you are alone in a room with language. It is not empty. It is the silence of a held bow before it is drawn across a string. Inside that silence, I can hear the faint hum of the refrigerator, the tick of a clock I did not know was in the room, the distant murmur of traffic like a river heard through stone. These sounds are also a kind of language. They say: the world continues. It does not pause for you to find the right word. It simply continues, and you either keep up or you do not.

I think about all the things I am not writing. The news. The names of people I have loved. The list of fears that visit me at 3 a.m. The small gods of worry and regret. They are here, in the room, but I am not giving them the chair. There is a discipline to stream-of-consciousness that no one talks about: you must choose which stream to follow. The mind offers many currents. Some are bright and swift. Some are dark and slow. Some lead to waterfalls. Some lead to stagnant pools. To write "whatever comes" is to practice a kind of selective surrender. You let go, but you also steer.

What comes now is the memory of a summer evening. I was young enough that time still felt enormous. The air smelled of cut grass and gasoline. A neighbor was mowing his lawn as the light turned gold. I sat on a porch step, watching the first bats flicker against the purple sky. I did not know the word "benediction" then, but I felt the thing itself: a blessing without a source. That moment did not need to be written. It was complete. And yet here it is, years later, reaching for language because I remember it. Maybe that is why we write: not to capture the moment, but to prove to ourselves that it mattered. The writing is the proof. The moment is the wound or the balm; the writing is the scar or the salve.

Now the light outside has shifted. It is no longer tea but honey. The bird has not returned. I am aware of the word count ticking down, and I feel a small thrill. There is a pleasure in limits. The sonnet, the haiku, the exactly one thousand words: they create a frame that makes the picture possible. Without the frame, the canvas is just a field. With it, the field becomes a window. I think of the poet who said, "I write in form because the form is a way of thinking." Or maybe I made that up. Either way, it feels true. The limit is not a cage; it is a spine. It gives the words something to stand on. I am running out of words now. The feeling is like approaching the end of a long exhale. What came was not a story, not an argument, not a poem. It was a record of a mind moving through a room of its own making. If it has any value, it is the value of the ordinary: attention held itself open, letting the world pass through. And now, at the end, what comes is gratitude. For the words. For the silence between them. For you, whoever read this far. That is enough. It always was. It is.
